entry.title: rabbitholes: how I built a Chrome extension with no server to touch your data
entry.summary: Most browser extensions that call external APIs route your data through a developer-controlled server first. That's not a conspiracy — it's the path of least resistance. You stand up a backend, proxy requests through it, log errors, maybe cache responses. The problem is that everything you highlight and every question you ask passes through infrastructure you don't control and the extension author probably didn't design for privacy from the start. rabbitholes does something different by construction: requests go directly from your browser to api.anthropic.com and api.search.brave.com. There is no intermediary server. There is nothing to log because there's nothing in the middle. This wasn't a late decision. The extension renders explanations in a shadow-DOM tooltip next to your cursor — the shadow DOM means the tooltip doesn't pollute the host page's styles or scripts. The same isolation principle runs through the data flow. Your Anthropic API key lives in chrome.storage.sync, which Chrome encrypts and syncs to your account. It never leaves the browser. The architecture made Manifest V3 compliance straightforward rather than painful. MV3 restricts remotely-hosted code and tightens background-service-worker lifetimes precisely because extensions were being used as attack surface. Building direct-to-API meant there was no server-side component to audit or trust. What the extension actually does: highlight any text on any page, get an explanation inline. Click any word in the explanation to go deeper — drag across words to pick a phrase. Every answer surfaces two suggested rabbit-hole topics. Hit the globe icon to re-answer enriched with Brave Search results, with source chips. A counter tracks how many hops deep you've gone. The privacy architecture isn't a feature I added. It's what you get when you start from "no server" and build outward. https://github.com/robertnowell/rabbitholes

entry.title: I built a demo for email personas – one inbox, multiple identities
entry.summary: Not a developer. Had an idea could not let go of. So just doing what I can. Here's my problem. Every time i want to start something new online — a business, a side project, anything — i need a new email address. But a new email address is not just a new address. It is a new account. And then i do it again for the next thing. Suddenly I am managing five separate lives across five separate accounts. I did not signed up for this. It just happened. I kept thinking: why does creating something new online require building an entirely new life around a new email account? Facebook already solved a version of this. You can be a person AND run a business on the same account. You switch between your personal Profile and your business Page in one tap. Same login. Same place. Different identity. Why has nobody done this for email? So I came up with something I am calling PersonaMail(for now). One account. One inbox. One login. But multiple personas — work, freelance, personal, business — each with its own address, its own sent history, its own identity. Switchable in a single tap. Just you — showing up as the right version of yourself, every time. I built a working demo to show what this could feel like. It is not code. It is not a startup. It is one person from a small city who saw a problem that millions of people have every day — and refused to accept that nobody had fixed it. 🔗 Try the demo: https://hj503x.github.io/Personamail/ If this frustration sounds familiar — I would love to hear from you. And if you know someone who should see this, please share it.

entry.summary: For a quarter century, the Google search box has been one of the most recognizable interfaces in computing: a thin white rectangle, a blinking cursor, a few typed words, and a list of blue links. On Tuesday, Google will formally retire that paradigm. At its annual I/O developer conference, Google announced a sweeping redesign of the search box itself — the literal text field where billions of queries begin every day — transforming it from a simple keyword input into a dynamic, AI-driven conversation starter that can accept text, images, PDFs, videos, and even open Chrome tabs as inputs.
